q-114429:
First, we select the identity that contains a $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Rearranging the above identity gives

$$
{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x-{sec}^{3}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\frac{(-\operatorname{sec}⁡x)({sec}^{2}⁡x-1)}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x{tan}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-[\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})] \\  & =-[2-\sqrt{2}] \\  & =\sqrt{2}-2\end{aligned}
$$

q-114457:
In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x.$ 

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{cot}^{5}⁡x-\operatorname{cot}⁡x}{(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{-\operatorname{cot}⁡x(1-{cot}^{4}⁡x)}{(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{-\operatorname{cot}⁡x(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)}{(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{-\operatorname{cot}⁡x{csc}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int -\operatorname{cot}⁡x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{csc}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-10567:
From the identity $1+{cot}^{2}⁡\theta ={csc}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =3x-2\pi ,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}1+{cot}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi ) & ={csc}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (7+4{x}^{3}+7{cot}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi ))\,\text{d}x & =\int (4{x}^{3}+7+7{cot}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi ))\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (4{x}^{3}+7[1+{cot}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi )])\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (4{x}^{3}+7{csc}^{2}⁡(3x-2\pi ))\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\cdot \frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+7(-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x-2\pi ))+C \\  & ={x}^{4}-\frac{7}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x-2\pi )+C.\end{aligned}
$$

q-13786:
If we let $u=-4x,$ then, 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4\,⟹\,-\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get the following:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $-4\operatorname{ln}⁡3$ |

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}5{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x & =5{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{-4x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{-4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{e}^{u}(-\frac{1}{4})\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}{\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{-4})}{e}^{u}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}({e}^{u}){|}_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{-4})} \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}({e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({3}^{-4})}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}({3}^{-4}-1) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(\frac{1}{{3}^{4}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(\frac{1}{81}-1) \\  & =-\frac{5}{4}(-\frac{80}{81}) \\  & =\frac{100}{81}\end{aligned}
$$

q-113833:
If we let $u=\frac{x}{2}-1,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,2\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {e}^{x/2\,-\,1}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{u}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int {e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\,{e}^{u}+C \\  & =2\,{e}^{x/2\,-\,1}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-31417:
If we let $u=\frac{x}{3},$ then,

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\text{d}u.
$$

Then, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {6}^{x/3}\,\text{d}x & =\int {6}^{u}\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\int {6}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\frac{{6}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C \\  & =\frac{3\cdot {6}^{x/3}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}+C\end{aligned}
$$

q-30973:
If we let $u=6x,$ then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u=\text{d}x.
$$

Computing our limits of integration, we get the following:

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $0$ | $6$ |

Then, we can write the integral in terms of  $u$ and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{3}^{6x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{6}{3}^{u}\cdot \frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{0}^{6}{3}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\frac{{3}^{u}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}){|}_{0}^{6} \\  & =\frac{1}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(729-1) \\  & =\frac{728}{6\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\  & =\frac{364}{3\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\end{aligned}
$$

q-51443:
The graph consists of $2$ parts: the line segment for $x\in [0,1]$ and the piecewise linear for $x\in [1,4].$ Therefore, we can write the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{1}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{2}}
$$

The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [0,1].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{1}=-1.
$$

The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [1,4].$ The corresponding region is a triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9 \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & =-{A}_{1}+{A}_{2} \\  & =-1+\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-14787:
The graph consists of $4$ parts: the line segment for $x\in [-4,-3]$, the line segment for $x\in [-3,0]$, the line segment for $x\in [0,2]$ and the two line segments for $x\in [2,6].$ Therefore, we can write the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-4}^{-3}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{-3}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{3}}+{{{\int }_{2}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{4}}
$$

The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-4,-3].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot 4 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-3,0].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
{\int }_{-3}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{2}=-\frac{9}{2}.
$$

The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [0,2].$ The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2+3)\cdot 2 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{3}=-5.
$$

The $4$th integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [2,6].$ The corresponding region is a trapezoid, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{4} & =\frac{1}{2}(a+b)h \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3+4)\cdot 2 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have 

$$
{\int }_{2}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{4}=-7.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{6}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}-{A}_{2}-{A}_{3}-{A}_{4} \\  & =2-\frac{9}{2}-5-7 \\  & =-\frac{29}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-49205:
The graph consists of $3$ parts: the line segment for $x\in [-4,-2],$ the line segment for $x\in [-2,0]$ and the arc of a semi-circle for $x\in [0,4].$ Therefore, we can write the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x={{{\int }_{-4}^{-2}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{{A}_{1}}+{{{\int }_{-2}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{2}}+{{{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x}_{⏟}}_{-{A}_{3}}
$$

The $1$st integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-4,-2].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

The $2$nd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [-2,0].$ The corresponding region is a right triangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}bh \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{2}=-2.
$$

The $3$rd integral represents the signed area between the curve and the $x$-axis, where $x\in [0,4].$ The corresponding region is a combination of a semi-circle and a rectangle, so we find the area using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{3} & =\frac{1}{2}\pi {r}^{2}+lw \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\pi \cdot {2}^{2}+4\cdot 2 \\  & =2\pi +8.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies below the $x$-axis, we have

$$
{\int }_{0}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x=-{A}_{3}=-2\pi -8.
$$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={A}_{1}-{A}_{2}-{A}_{3} \\  & =2-2-2\pi -8 \\  & =-2\pi -8.\end{aligned}
$$

q-40270:
To solve the inequality $P(x)>0,$ we need to find the values of $x$ for which the curve $y=P(x)$ lies above the $x$-axis.

The roots of the polynomial $P(x)=(x+2)(x-1)(x-2)$ are $x=1$ and $x=\pm 2,$ which are all simple roots.

Also, $P(x)$ is a cubic polynomial with a positive leading coefficient. So, we can graph the curve as follows:

q-87672:
To solve the inequality $P(x)>0,$ we need to find the values of $x$ for which the curve $y=P(x)$ lies above the $x$-axis.

First, we factor the polynomial $P(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x) & =12{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}-{x}^{4} \\  & =-({x}^{4}-{x}^{3}-12{x}^{2}) \\  & =-{x}^{2}({x}^{2}-x-12) \\  & =-{x}^{2}({x}^{2}-4x+3x-12) \\  & =-{x}^{2}(x(x-4)+3(x-4)) \\  & =-{x}^{2}(x+3)(x-4)\end{aligned}
$$

The roots of the polynomial $P(x)=12{x}^{2}+{x}^{3}-{x}^{4}$ are $x=-3,$ $x=0$ and $x=4,$ where

- $x=0$ has multiplicity $2,$ and

- $x=-3$ and $x=4$ are simple roots.

So, we can graph the curve as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14007649/assets/5ebfbd4e18de00fad05c4192be2147a9b9765e00fae5b74ac608e85466c21e73.png)

Since we are interested in solving $P(x)>0,$ we look for the part of the curve that is above the $x$-axis.

Based on the graph, the solution is 

$$
x\in (-3,0)\cup (0,4).
$$

q-106447:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-1,2),$ and passes through the point $(1,4).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-1,2),$ and so we have

$$
x+1=2pt,\,y-2=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(1,4),$ we can substitute $x=1$ and $y=4$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}2=2pt \\ 2=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2pt \\ 1 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{1}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =p{(\frac{1}{p})}^{2} \\ 2 & =p\cdot \frac{1}{{p}^{2}} \\ 2 & =\frac{1}{p} \\ p & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+1=2(\frac{1}{2})t,\,y-2=(\frac{1}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+1=t,\,y-2=\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$

q-106452:
The diagram shows that the parabola is vertical, has its vertex at $(-2,-3),$ and passes through the point $(-12,-13).$

The parametric equations of a vertical parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=2pt,\,y-k=p{t}^{2},
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,-3),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=2pt,\,y+3=p{t}^{2}.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(-12,-13),$ we can substitute $x=-12$ and $y=-13$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}-10=2pt \\ -10=p{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-10 & =2pt \\ -5 & =pt \\ t & =-\frac{5}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the second equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-10 & =p{(-\frac{5}{p})}^{2} \\ -10 & =p\cdot \frac{25}{{p}^{2}} \\ -10 & =\frac{25}{p} \\ p & =-\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=2(-\frac{5}{2})t,\,y+3=(-\frac{5}{2}){t}^{2},
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=-5t,\,y+3=-\frac{5}{2}{t}^{2}.
$$

q-106459:
The diagram shows that the parabola is horizontal, has its vertex at $(-2,3),$ and passes through the point $(6,11).$

The parametric equations of a horizontal parabola that has its vertex at $(h,k)$ are

$$
x-h=p{t}^{2},\,y-k=2pt,
$$

where $p$ is constant.

In our case, $(h,k)=(-2,3),$ and so we have

$$
x+2=p{t}^{2},\,y-3=2pt.
$$

Since the parabola passes through $(6,11),$ we can substitute $x=6$ and $y=11$ into the parametric equations to obtain a system of equations. This gives

$$
{\begin{aligned}8=p{t}^{2} \\ 8=2pt.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the second equation for $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =2pt \\ 4 & =pt \\ t & =\frac{4}{p}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the first equation and solving for $p,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8 & =p{(\frac{4}{p})}^{2} \\ 8 & =p\cdot \frac{16}{{p}^{2}} \\ 8 & =\frac{16}{p} \\ p & =\frac{16}{8} \\ p & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the parametric equations of the parabola are

$$
x+2=(2){t}^{2},\,y-3=2(2)t,
$$

which simplify to

$$
x+2=2{t}^{2},\,y-3=4t.
$$
